name: Seselwa Creole French
confidence_why: 2 independent first-hand sources agree (1 agree, 0 refine), none contradicts

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: Coding 'fixed-dominant' (final stress, non-strict because of speech-act-conditioned initial stress in isolated imperatives) rests on Michaelis & Rosalie 2013 (APiCS survey ch. 56). We held no copy; I downloaded the online chapter and the deciding sentence is there verbatim (only the accent on 'déor' is missing in our quote), and the chapter adds that Seychellois lacks the Mauritian réfer/refér stress contrast, which supports final stress as the sole lexical pattern. The source is a short survey sketch but by the language's principal academic describer, dated 2013; Glottolog's fuller items are two 1977 grammars (Bollée, Corne) that we do not hold and that are paywalled/print-only; no phonology article, instrumental study or JIPA Illustration exists as far as web searches show, and the one open dissertation (Brück 2016) is silent on stress. Nothing suggests the classification is wrong; the record's g

sources.citation: Michaelis & Rosalie, APiCS Online survey ch. 56, re-read at apics-online.info/surveys/56; imperative first-syllable cases are speech-act-conditioned, not lexical
sources.quote: Word stress is always on the last syllable. In some contexts where isolated words are uttered in an imperative speech act, we may find the stress on the first syllable, e.g. deor 'get out of here' ('outside')

sources.citation: Michaelis, Susanne Maria & Rosalie, Marcel. 2013. Seychelles Creole. In Michaelis, Maurer, Haspelmath & Huber (eds.), The Survey of Pidgin and Creole Languages, vol. II. Oxford: OUP. Online version: APiCS Online survey chapter 56, https://apics-online.info/surveys/56
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: Word stress is always on the last syllable. In some contexts where isolated words are uttered in an imperative speech act, we may find the stress on the first syllable, e.g. déor 'get out of here', dévan 'in front!'. ... there is no stress opposition as found in Mauritian Creole (réfer vs refér); in Seychelles Creole both verbs show stress on the last syllable.
